chunks.text: European maritime empires were empires built not by marching across neighboring land but by crossing oceans and projecting power across the globe by sea. They were the political and economic framework of the early-modern global age, c. 1450–1750.

In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with about 600 men and within two years toppled the Aztec Empire of millions, whose capital Tenochtitlan was larger than most European cities. Spanish numbers alone could not explain this.

A few hundred Spaniards overthrew the Aztec and Inca empires because of devastating smallpox epidemics that gutted Native populations and leadership, Spanish steel weapons, horses, and gunpowder, and alliances with indigenous peoples who resented Aztec or Inca domination. Cortés's army was overwhelmingly indigenous.

In the early 1530s Francisco Pizarro, with an even smaller force than Cortés, toppled the vast Inca Empire of the Andes, again aided by epidemic disease, superior weapons and horses, and exploitation of internal divisions.

In the Americas, Europeans built territorial empires, conquering and ruling vast lands directly. Spain seized the former Aztec and Inca heartlands and much of Central and South America, and Portugal claimed Brazil; these were settler-and-extraction empires exploiting silver, land, and labor.

In Asia and along the African coast, Europeans built trading-post empires: networks of fortified coastal ports from which they controlled trade routes rather than large territories. They could not conquer the powerful land empires of the region, so they operated as armed merchants at the choke-points of trade.

The Portuguese pioneered the trading-post empire, seizing key Indian Ocean ports such as Goa, Malacca, and Hormuz and trying to tax and control the spice trade by force. They were soon challenged and largely displaced by the Dutch and English.

Europeans took territory in the Americas because epidemics and the lack of indigenous gunpowder and horses made conquest possible, but controlled only ports in Asia because the Ottoman, Mughal, and Ming/Qing empires were militarily formidable and economically self-sufficient.

Mercantilism was the guiding economic philosophy of the maritime empires. Mercantilists believed national wealth depended on accumulating gold and silver and maintaining a favorable balance of trade. Colonies existed to serve the mother country, supplying raw materials and buying its manufactured goods.

The joint-stock company was a business in which many investors pooled their money and shared the profits and risks, letting Europeans raise vast capital for risky overseas ventures while spreading risk. It is the ancestor of the modern corporation.

The Dutch East India Company (VOC, founded 1602) and the English East India Company (EIC, founded 1600) were the most powerful joint-stock companies. Chartered by their governments, they could wage war, build forts, negotiate treaties, and govern territory, and the EIC would eventually rule much of India.

The Spanish discovered enormous silver deposits in the Americas, above all at Potosí in modern Bolivia, worked by brutally coerced indigenous labor. American silver became the first truly global currency.

Much American silver ended up in China, because the Ming and Qing required taxes to be paid in silver, creating an almost limitless demand. Silver flowed across the Atlantic via Europe and across the Pacific via the Spanish Manila galleons (Mexico to the Philippines) in exchange for Chinese silk, porcelain, and tea.

The silver trade tied the Americas, Europe, and Asia into a single continuous global economy for the first time. Silver mined in the Americas flowed to China for luxury goods, making global integration visible in one commodity.

So much American silver flooded into Europe that it caused inflation, known as the 'price revolution,' an unintended economic effect of the silver trade that raised prices across Europe over the 1500s and 1600s.

The encomienda was an early Spanish American labor system in which the crown granted colonists the right to demand labor and tribute from indigenous people in a given area. It was slavery in all but name and a major driver of indigenous death.

As the indigenous population collapsed, the encomienda gave way to systems including the hacienda (large estates worked by laborers, often in debt peonage) and the silver mita, a coercive labor draft adapted from Inca practice to force indigenous men to work the mines.

Atlantic chattel slavery, centered on enslaved Africans, was the most consequential new labor system. The enslaved person was legal property, the status was inherited by children, and it became rigidly tied to race. Roughly 12 million Africans were carried across the Atlantic in the Middle Passage.

Indentured servitude was a labor system in which a laborer worked for a fixed number of years, often in exchange for passage to the Americas, before gaining freedom. Unlike chattel slavery it was temporary and not hereditary, and it supplied additional workers, especially Europeans in some colonies.

The Atlantic system, or triangular trade, was a circuit tying three continents: European manufactured goods and guns shipped to Africa, enslaved Africans carried across the Middle Passage to the Americas, and American plantation commodities (sugar, tobacco, cotton) and silver shipped back to Europe.

European maritime power in Asia rested on combining ocean-going ships with heavy cannon, letting small Atlantic kingdoms dominate coastal choke-points without conquering bordering empires. For most of this period Asia's land empires were still wealthier and more populous, and Europeans paid for Asian goods largely in American silver.
